newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch swine fever toll mounts, pork prices rise.
newsitem.headline: Dutch swine fever toll mounts, pork prices rise.

text.p: Two more cases of swine fever emerged in the Netherlands on Tuesday, and the country's leading retailer said it was increasing pork prices.

The Dutch Farm Ministry said the disease had been detected at two more farms, taking the total affected to 133, 12 more than a week ago. Around one million pigs have so far been destroyed in a bid to control the highly contagious disease, which is not harmful to humans.

Leading Dutch retail chain Albert Heijn said it had been forced to raise its pork prices this week by one guilder a kilo in response to a meat shortage that has sent wholesale market prices to all-time highs.
"We have had to take the step because the prices we have to pay have gone up so much," a spokesman said.
Prices paid by Dutch slaughterhouses for live pigs have exceeded five guilders a kilo for the first time ever. At the start of the year, pigs were fetching just three guilders.
"This will certainly not be the last price increase we see in the near future. We haven't reached the top yet," the Albert Heijn spokesman said.
The government has imposed strict controls on the pig sector in a bid to stamp out the latest swine fever outbreak, detected in February and the first to hit the country for five years.
Governmment efforts have included imposing a transport ban on livestock and pig manure and semen in almost half the country and strict checks on all pig farms nationwide.
The army has been called in to help with the transport of animals to slaughterhouses.
The cost to the farming industry is believed to be running close to one billion guilders.
The Netherlands has lost key export revenue because of the disease, which prompted the European Union to impose a ban on Dutch pig exports.
Many countries, including the U.S., have extended the ban to imports of Dutch pork products.
Pig and pork exports were worth more than five billion guilders to the Netherlands last year.
According to a report from the U.S. embassy in The Hague this week, Dutch exports of live pigs would be cut by half this year, possibly opening up a new market for U.S. exporters.

"The hog cholera (swine fever) crisis theoretically provides the opportunity for the United States to export live pigs to the European Union," the report said. However, it added that meeting strict EU import requirements, such as whole herd testing, would probably make such a move prohibitive on a cost basis.

"Because new cases continue to occur regularly, there is not a lot of optimism the hog cholera crisis will be over soon," the report said, adding the EU export and internal transport bans were expected to remain in place for several months.
